title: Doob's martingale convergence theorems
body: In mathematics – specifically, in the theory of stochastic processes – Doob's martingale convergence theorems are a collection of results on the limits of supermartingales, named after the American mathematician Joseph L. Doob. Informally, the martingale convergence theorem typically refers to the result that any supermartingale satisfying a certain boundedness condition must converge. One may think of supermartingales as the random variable analogues of non-increasing sequences; from this perspective, the martingale convergence theorem is a random variable analogue of the monotone convergence theorem, which states that any bounded monotone sequence converges. There are symmetric results for submartingales, which are analogous to non-decreasing sequences.

title: de la Vallee Poussin Criterion for Uniform Integrability
body:
Let (Omega, F, P) be a probability space and {X_i : i in I} a family of random variables. The family is uniformly integrable if and only if there exists a nondecreasing convex function G : [0, infinity) -> [0, infinity) with G(t)/t -> infinity as t -> infinity such that sup_{i in I} E[G(|X_i|)] < infinity. The sufficiency direction is the one used in practice: a uniform bound on any superlinear moment, for example sup_i E[|X_i|^p] < infinity for a single p > 1, or sup_i E[|X_i| log^+ |X_i|] < infinity, forces uniform integrability. A uniform bound on the FIRST moment does not: on ([0,1], Lebesgue) the family X_n = n 1_{(0,1/n)} has E|X_n| = 1 for all n and is not uniformly integrable. [standard; e.g. Dellacherie and Meyer, Probabilities and Potential, or Williams, Probability with Martingales, Section 13.3]
a probability space (or a finite measure space)
G convex, nondecreasing, superlinear at infinity; the constant sup_i E[G(|X_i|)] must be uniform over the family

title: Doob's Martingale Convergence Theorem (a.s. Convergence Under an L^1 Bound)
body:
Let (X_n) be a submartingale with sup_n E[X_n^+] < infinity. Then X_n converges almost surely to a limit X_infinity with E|X_infinity| < infinity. For a MARTINGALE the hypothesis is equivalent to sup_n E|X_n| < infinity, since E[X_n] is constant and E|X_n| = 2E[X_n^+] - E[X_n]. Convergence is ONLY almost sure: it need not hold in L^1, and E[X_infinity] need not equal E[X_0]. Standard failure: let (X_n) be the product of independent nonnegative mean-one factors, for instance X_n = prod_{k <= n} (1 + eps_k) with eps_k = +1 or -1 with probability 1/2 each - equivalently X_n = 2^n on the event that all signs were +1 and 0 otherwise. Then X_n is a nonnegative martingale with E X_n = 1 for every n, so it is L^1-bounded and converges a.s., but the limit is 0 almost surely and E X_infinity = 0 != 1 = E X_0. Nonnegative supermartingales always converge a.s. because X_n^+ = X_n has bounded expectation; upgrading to L^1 convergence is exactly what uniform integrability supplies. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.2.11]
(X_n) a submartingale for a filtration (F_n)
sup_n E[X_n^+] < infinity (for a martingale: sup_n E|X_n| < infinity)
no uniform integrability is assumed, and without it convergence is only almost sure

title: Levy's Downward Theorem (Backward Martingale Convergence)
body:
Let (G_n)_{n >= 0} be a DECREASING family of sub-sigma-algebras, G_0 containing G_1 containing G_2 and so on, and let G_infinity be their intersection. For Y in L^1, E[Y | G_n] converges almost surely and in L^1 to E[Y | G_infinity]. More generally a BACKWARD MARTINGALE, a family (X_n) with X_n G_n-measurable and E[X_n | G_{n+1}] = X_{n+1}, converges almost surely and in L^1 - and unlike the forward case NO extra hypothesis is required, because a backward martingale is automatically uniformly integrable: X_n = E[X_0 | G_n] is a family of conditional expectations of one integrable variable. This asymmetry with the forward theorem is the point: forward martingales need an L^1 bound for almost sure convergence and uniform integrability for L^1 convergence, backward martingales need neither. The classical application is the strong law of large numbers: with S_n the partial sums of an i.i.d. integrable sequence and G_n the exchangeable sigma-algebra generated by S_n, S_{n+1}, ..., one has E[X_1 | G_n] = S_n/n, so S_n/n converges almost surely and in L^1, and the Hewitt-Savage 0-1 law identifies the limit as E[X_1]. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.6.1]
(G_n) decreasing with intersection G_infinity
Y integrable, or (X_n) a backward martingale with X_0 integrable

title: Biskup's Conjecture 16.5 (size of deep extremal level sets of the 2D DGFF) is equivalent to his Conjecture 16.6 given uniform integrability of deep cluster sizes
body:
PRIVATE REDUCTION, author-recorded. By the cluster-process structure of the DGFF extremal process (Biskup-Louidor), the number of points of the level set at depth t inside A is a Poisson sum over extremal local maxima in A of i.i.d. cluster sizes at the corresponding depths, so its conditional expectation given the extremal measure Z^D equals Z^D(A) times the integral over depth of e^{alpha s} E[cluster size at depth s] ds. Conjecture 16.5 (the count normalised by (1/t) e^{-alpha t} converges to c Z^D(A)) therefore reduces to the existence of lim e^{-alpha h} E_nu(f_h) (Conjecture 16.6) plus (i) uniform integrability of cluster sizes at depth t uniformly in N, to exchange the N and t limits, and (ii) a variance bound making the Poisson sum concentrate, which follows from the same uniform integrability. Conversely 16.5 implies the limit in 16.6 by taking expectations. The open content is thus 16.6 together with the uniform-in-N control of deep clusters, which the concentric decomposition delivers only at bounded depth.
2D DGFF in admissible domains; extremal process with Poisson-cluster structure (Biskup-Louidor)
Exchange of limits requires uniform integrability not currently available

title: Technique: Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer Branching Process with Migration
body:
TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For one-dimensional nearest-neighbor random walk in an i.i.d. random environment in the subballistic or intermediate regime, parametrized by an index kappa solving E[rho^kappa]=1 for rho the local odds ratio of the environment, hitting times of successive integers admit a classical Kesten construction as a branching process with migration: individuals reproduce according to an environment-dependent offspring law with an added immigration/emigration term reflecting the local environment. The Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer theorem shows that for kappa in the relevant range below 2, the hitting time of level n, normalized by n^{1/kappa}, converges to a kappa-stable distribution, via a result on the total population size of the associated branching-with-migration process, which itself has heavy-tailed, stable-scaling behavior. This gives the precise non-Gaussian scaling limits characterizing anomalous, subdiffusive or index-dependent, behavior in one-dimensional random walk in random environment, a phenomenon absent for simple random walk. It does not extend to higher dimensions, since the explicit branching correspondence is a genuinely one-dimensional, nearest-neighbor phenomenon, and it requires the environment to be i.i.d. with a moment condition admitting a solution kappa in the relevant range. Typical failure: Extending the branching-process-with-migration correspondence and its kappa-stable scaling conclusion to multi-dimensional random walk in random environment, or to environments with dependence rather than i.i.d. structure, where no analogous exact combinatorial bijection to a branching process is known; the Kesten construction is a special, essentially exact identity in one dimension that does not generalize by analogy, so claiming kappa-stable scaling outside the one-dimensional i.i.d. setting requires an entirely separate justification. Canonical reference: Kesten, Kozlov and Spitzer, 1975, Compositio Mathematica.
one-dimensional, nearest-neighbor random walk in an i.i.d. random environment
existence of kappa in (0,2) solving E[rho^kappa]=1 for the environment's local odds ratio rho
transience of the walk, or the appropriate directional condition for the regime under study
technical non-lattice or non-degeneracy conditions on the environment law needed for the stable-law convergence

title: Uniform Integrability of Random Variables
body:
A family \{X_i : i \in I\} of real-valued random variables is uniformly integrable if \lim_{M \to \infty} \sup_{i \in I} \mathbb{E}[|X_i| \mathbf{1}_{\{|X_i| > M\}}] = 0. Equivalently: (1) \sup_{i \in I} \mathbb{E}[|X_i|] < \infty; and (2) for every \epsilon > 0, there exists \delta > 0 such that \mathbb{P}(A) < \delta implies \sup_{i \in I} \mathbb{E}[|X_i| \mathbf{1}_A] < \epsilon.
\{X_i\} family of random variables on a common probability space

title: L2 Martingale Convergence for Repeated k-Averages
body:
Let tau = 1 - (k-1)/(n-1). The scaled process M_l = S_n(l) / tau^l is a non-negative martingale with respect to F_l, and lim_{l->infty} M_l exists and is finite almost surely.
tau = 1 - (k-1)/(n-1) > 0

title: de la Vallee-Poussin criterion for uniform integrability
body:
Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a finite measure space and let F be a subset of L^1(mu). Then F is uniformly integrable if and only if there exists a nondecreasing convex function Phi on [0, infinity) with Phi(0) = 0 and Phi(t)/t tending to infinity as t tends to infinity, such that sup over f in F of integral Phi(|f|) dmu is finite. The 'if' direction is the one used in practice: a uniform bound on a superlinear moment forces uniform integrability.
mu finite.
Phi must be convex, nondecreasing and superlinear (Phi(t)/t to infinity);
mere growth of Phi is not enough.

title: Known false (branching random walk): uniform integrability of the derivative martingale is not equivalent to a positive limit; E dW_n = 0, so UI forces the limit to vanish - the right word is nondegenerate
body: Conjecture 3.2 of arXiv:2608.21125 says the derivative martingale is uniformly integrable 'equivalently' its limit is positive; those are incompatible - UI forces the limit to vanish since E[dW_n]=0 and the limit is nonnegative. Repaired to 'nondegenerate', the martingale half is a theorem in the bounded-degree regime by Chen's criterion

title: Uniform integrability
body: A family $\{X_i\}$ of integrable random variables is uniformly integrable if $\lim_{M\to\infty}\sup_iE[|X_i|1\{|X_i|>M\}]=0$; with convergence in probability it is equivalent to $L^1$ convergence, and a UI martingale is closed by its a.s. limit.

title: Janson 20.1: uniform integrability at a fixed level
body:
[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked, no independent read] This is the finite-moment part of Svante Janson's Conjecture 20.1 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Let pi = (pi_j)_{j>=0} be a nondegenerate offspring law on the nonnegative integers with pi_0 > 0, sum j pi_j = 1, and variance sigma^2 in (0,infinity). Let xi have law pi, let T be the ordered Galton-Watson tree in which all vertices independently have pi-distributed numbers of children, and let T_n have the law of T conditional on its total number of vertices being n, along admissible n for which that event has positive probability. For a rooted tree A define ell_k(A) as its number of vertices at graph distance k from the root. Define the Kesten tree T_hat by an infinite distinguished spine: a spine vertex has j children with probability j pi_j, one uniformly selected child continues the spine, and every other child starts an independent ordinary pi Galton-Watson tree. Fix an integer k >= 1. If r >= 1 is real and E[xi^(r+1)] < infinity, then the family {ell_k(T_n)^r}_n is uniformly integrable and E[ell_k(T_n)^r] -> E[ell_k(T_hat)^r] < infinity. Here uniform integrability means lim_{K->infinity} sup_n E[ell_k(T_n)^r; ell_k(T_n)^r > K] = 0. For 0 < r < 1 the same conclusion follows under the displayed finite-variance assumption. The critical infinite-variance case with 0 < r < 1 is not settled by this result. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
pi is critical, nondegenerate, and pi_0 > 0.
k is fixed and positive; conditioning sizes are admissible.
For r >= 1, E[xi^(r+1)] < infinity; for 0 < r < 1, Var(xi) < infinity.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:bd2d999d3e00a51463fc179469341fd2dc4ce15d9ff3e743bb7fd43377460681","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/bd/bd2d999d3e00a51463fc179469341fd2dc4ce15d9ff3e743bb7fd43377460681.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:9d13417b75738e2fc15d10e3322f651494c6abbbfcb1c6c7d810fcc69a74ead5","bundle_entry_key":"janson-conjecture-20-1-fixed-level-moment-convergence","bundle_id":"population.probability-campaign-results-20260914-001","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-prob1000-nodes-1010/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.trees:janson-conjecture-20-1-fixed-level-moment-convergence","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Write $n$ for the tree sizes along which $T_n$ is defined ($n \equiv 1 \pmod{\text{span}}$) and $S_M$ for the sum of $M$ i.i.d. copies of $\xi \sim \pi$, so $\mathbb{E}\xi = 1$ and $\sigma^2 < \infty$. Two facts about $S_M$: by the local limit theorem for lattice laws with finite variance,
$$\mathbb{P}(S_n = n - 1) \ge c\,n^{-1/2} \quad\text{for all admissible } n, \qquad \sup_j \mathbb{P}(S_M = j) \le C\,M^{-1/2} \quad\text{for all } M \ge 1, \tag{1}$$
with $c, C > 0$ depending on $\pi$ only (the second holds for large $M$ by the same theorem and for the remaining $M$ trivially).

*The weight of a truncated tree.* Let $t$ be a finite plane tree whose vertices of depth less than $k$ have prescribed outdegrees and whose vertices at depth $k$ are leaves of $t$ with unspecified subtrees; call the former the interior $I(t)$, put $N = |I(t)| = 1 + \ell_1(t) + \dots + \ell_{k-1}(t)$ and $\ell = \ell_k(t)$. Let $T^{(k)}$ denote a tree truncated at depth $k$. For $\ell \ge 1$ and $n > N$, Lemma 14.9 of the survey (with the interior vertices as $v_1, \dots, v_N$ in depth-first order, $\sum_{i \le N} d_i = N - 1 + \ell$) gives
$$\mathbb{P}\big(T_n^{(k)} = t\big) = \ell\,\frac{n}{n - N}\,\mathbb{P}(Y_i = d_i,\ i \le N),$$
where $(Y_1, \dots, Y_n)$ is the allocation $B_{n-1,n}$, i.e. $n$ i.i.d. copies of $\xi$ conditioned on $S_n = n - 1$; so
$$\mathbb{P}\big(T_n^{(k)} = t\big) = \mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{GW}}\big(T^{(k)} = t\big)\;W_n(t), \qquad W_n(t) := \frac{n\,\ell\;\mathbb{P}(S_{n-N} = n - N - \ell)}{(n - N)\;\mathbb{P}(S_n = n - 1)}, \tag{2}$$
with $\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{GW}}(T^{(k)} = t) = \prod_{v \in I(t)}\pi_{d(v)}$ the probability that the first $k$ generations of the unconditioned Galton–Watson tree $T$ are $t$. (The formula is also the cycle lemma applied to the forest of $\ell$ subtrees with $n - N$ vertices in total; the survey proves it from Lemma 14.3.) If $\ell = 0$ then $t$ is a whole tree and contributes nothing to any expectation of $\ell_k^r$ on $\{\ell_k \ge 1\}$, so it can be ignored.

Two bounds follow from (1) and (2). First,
$$W_n(t) \le \frac{n\,\ell\,C (n-N)^{-1/2}}{(n-N)\,c\,n^{-1/2}} = C'\,\ell\Big(\frac{n}{n-N}\Big)^{3/2}, \qquad C' = C/c. \tag{3}$$
Second, since the $\ell$ vertices at depth $k$ are among the $n - N$ vertices outside the interior, $n - N \ge \ell$, and so
$$W_n(t) \le C'\,n^{3/2}\,\ell^{-1/2}. \tag{4}$$

*Moments of generation sizes of the unconditioned tree.* For $s \ge 1$ and $Z_j := \ell_j(T)$: given $Z_{j-1} = m$, $Z_j$ is a sum of $m$ i.i.d. copies of $\xi$, so by Minkowski $\mathbb{E}[Z_j^s \mid Z_{j-1} = m] \le m^s\,\mathbb{E}\xi^s$, hence $\mathbb{E} Z_j^s \le (\mathbb{E}\xi^s)^j < \infty$ when $\mathbb{E}\xi^s < \infty$. Likewise $\mathbb{E}[Z_k^s \mid Z_j = m] \le m^s(\mathbb{E}\xi^s)^{k-j}$ for $s \ge 1$, and for $0 < s < 1$ by Jensen $\mathbb{E}[Z_k^s \mid Z_j = m] \le (\mathbb{E}[Z_k \mid Z_j = m])^s = m^s$ (mean one). So in all cases, for $0 < s \le r + 1$,
$$\mathbb{E}[Z_k^s \mid Z_j = m] \le C_s\,m^s. \tag{5}$$

*Uniform integrability.* Fix $K > 1$. By (2),
$$\mathbb{E}\big[\ell_k(T_n)^r;\ \ell_k(T_n) > K\big] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{GW}}\big[Z_k^r\,W_n(T^{(k)});\ Z_k > K\big],$$
where on the right $N = N_k := 1 + Z_1 + \dots + Z_{k-1}$ is the number of vertices of $T$ of depth less than $k$. Split according to $N_k \le n/2$ or $N_k > n/2$.

On $\{N_k \le n/2\}$, (3) gives $W_n \le 2^{3/2}C' Z_k$, so this part is at most
$$2^{3/2}C'\;\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{GW}}\big[Z_k^{r+1};\ Z_k > K\big],$$
which does not depend on $n$ and tends to $0$ as $K \to \infty$ because $\mathbb{E} Z_k^{r+1} \le (\mathbb{E}\xi^{r+1})^k < \infty$.

On $\{N_k > n/2\}$, (4) gives $Z_k^r W_n \le C' n^{3/2} Z_k^{r - 1/2}$, and $N_k > n/2$ forces $Z_j > n/(2k)$ for some $1 \le j \le k - 1$ when $n > 2k$ (the root alone cannot do it). So this part is at most
$$C' n^{3/2}\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{GW}}\big[Z_k^{r-1/2};\ Z_j > n/(2k)\big] \le C' C_{r-1/2}\,n^{3/2}\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{GW}}\big[Z_j^{r-1/2};\ Z_j > n/(2k)\big]$$
by (5) with $s = r - 1/2 \in [1/2, r+1]$, and on $\{Z_j > n/(2k)\}$ we have $Z_j^{r-1/2} \le (2k/n)^{3/2} Z_j^{r+1}$, so the whole thing is at most
$$C' C_{r-1/2}\,(2k)^{3/2}\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{GW}}\big[Z_j^{r+1};\ Z_j > n/(2k)\big] \longrightarrow 0 \quad (n \to \infty),$$
again because $\mathbb{E} Z_j^{r+1} < \infty$. This part does not depend on $K$ at all.

Hence $\limsup_{n}\mathbb{E}[\ell_k(T_n)^r; \ell_k(T_n) > K] \le 2^{3/2}C'\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{GW}}[Z_k^{r+1}; Z_k > K] \to 0$ as $K \to \infty$, and since each $\mathbb{E}\,\ell_k(T_n)^r$ is finite (a finite tree), the family $\{\ell_k(T_n)^r\}$ is uniformly integrable. Together with $\ell_k(T_n) \to_d \ell_k(\widehat T)$, (20.1) of the survey, this gives $\mathbb{E}\,\ell_k(T_n)^r \to \mathbb{E}\,\ell_k(\widehat T)^r$, and the limit is finite because the moments are bounded. $\square$

Consequently Conjecture 20.1 holds for every integer $r \ge 1$ and, more generally, for every real $r \ge 1$; for $0 < r < 1$ it holds whenever $\sigma^2 < \infty$ (then $\ell_k(T_n)$ itself is uniformly integrable by the case $r = 1$, and so is any smaller power).
